set.overview: A two-pitch 5.10 on Easter Island, one of the small sandstone towers on the ridge between Bridger Jack Mesa and the Butte in Indian Creek. The opening pitch is a moderate stretch of jamming, around 5.8, that leads to a traverse right around the nose. Above that the route turns to face climbing, which is unusual in a crack-dominated area. The tower was the last in its group to be climbed.
set.approach: Drive into Indian Creek, take the signed Beef Basin Road, ford the river and pass the cattle guard, then turn right at once and follow the dirt road until the serrated ridge of Bridger Jack rises directly overhead. A truck is preferred, though low cars have made it. A large cairn between two campsites marks the trail that climbs to the base of the towers; walk the base trail to Easter Island.
hazards: Sandstone is weak when wet, so skip it during and after rain
Seasonal raptor closures in spring; confirm current areas with the land manager before climbing
Few toilet facilities at the base, so pack out waste

review.notes: Descent skipped: only a photo caption shows a rappel, no anchor or rope details. Season, gain and distance skipped (no page states them). Approach is the Bridger Jacks area approach, not Easter Island specific.

set.approach: Drive into Indian Creek and turn left onto the signed Beef Basin Road, then ford the river, pass the cattle guard, turn right immediately, and follow the road to the point beneath the serrated ridge of Bridger Jack. A large cairn between two campsites marks the trail to the base of the towers. King of Pain is the tall twin-summited tower; the line starts on its south side below the notch beside Hummingbird Spire.
hazards: Loose rock around the notch on the second pitch
Stuck ropes are common on the east-face rappels
Sandstone is fragile when wet, so avoid climbing after rain
Spring raptor closures apply in the area; check current limits first

review.notes: Descent is assembled from the neighbouring Sacred Space and Vision Quest pages (same tower, the route joins Sacred Space at the notch), not from a page on Egg Drop Soup itself. Gain, distance, season skipped.

set.overview: A single 165-foot pitch up the southwest arete of Thumbelina, which is the leftmost of the detached towers in the Bridger Jack group. It begins in a wide crack, about 5.6, then follows a bolted arete with face moves that feel more like gym climbing than Indian Creek splitters. There are several rests and some bouldery sections, a lower crux around 10+/11-, and a harder upper crux at the last two bolts before a mantle onto the summit.
set.approach: Drive into Indian Creek, take the signed Beef Basin Road, ford the river and pass the cattle guard, then turn right and follow the dirt road to the foot of the serrated Bridger Jack ridge. Take the obvious trail along the base of the cliff all the way to the left end, where the route starts in the wide crack leading to the left arete. A 50 m rope may need you to belay right at its base.
set.descent_text: Rappel from the summit with a double-rope setup. The tower is a short detached spire, so the rappel goes straight to the ground at its base; walk back along the base trail to the car.
hazards: Desperate moves at the last two bolts for many climbers
Sandstone is damaged easily when wet; avoid it after rain
Raptor closures in spring; verify with the land manager
Summit mantle exits onto a small top, so commit carefully

review.notes: Season, gain, distance skipped. The sentence about rappelling straight to the ground is an inference from the single 165 ft route length; the page only says double-rope rappel. Trim if the reviewer dislikes it.

set.approach: From the Castleton and Rectory trail junction in Castle Valley, walk along the Rectory's west side. For most routes you continue all the way around the Priest and come back a short distance to the base of the Nuns, about 15 minutes in total. The Nuns are the two short semi-detached towers at the north end of the Rectory.
hazards: Wet sandstone breaks and is permanently damaged; do not climb during or after rain
Spring raptor closures happen every year; check the current closure list before you go

review.notes: Descent, gain, distance and season skipped: no page opened states them for this route. Approach is the Nuns area approach.

set.approach: Turn off State Route 14 onto Indian Wells Canyon Road a short way beyond Indian Wells and drive the dirt road to the wilderness barricade, roughly 7.7 miles from the highway. Parts are rough and rutted, so high clearance helps. The trailhead sits near 5,440 feet. Walk the old road past the barricade, where it becomes a canyon trail, to a clearing near 6,100 feet, then take the right fork.
set.descent_text: Return the way you came. Pick your way down the steep slabs and the dark boulder field following the ducks, and watch for the spot near 7,400 feet where climbers drift onto white talus instead of the main use trail. The trail is easier to follow downhill. Below the clearing it eases back to the old road and the barricade.
hazards: Steep granite slabs are slippery and should be avoided with snow or ice on them
Wrong turn near 7,400 feet onto white boulders leads to exposed class 3
Deadfall can block the canyon trail in places
Rough, rutted access road

evidence.fact: 3,200 ft total gain (3,100 up, 100 on return)
about 3,306 ft gain to 8,453 ft summit

review.notes: Distance skipped: one source says about 7 miles round trip, the other 5.9 miles (16% apart). Season skipped: no page states a window.

set.approach: Drive Canebrake Road to the saddle where the Lamont Peak Trail begins, near 5,500 feet, where several cars can park. The trail leaves the saddle and climbs the ridge steeply. It is faint in spots and marked by cairns, but it is always good enough to follow, so avoid striking off into the brush. Higher up it leads to the summit rocks.
set.descent_text: Return down the same trail. It is steep, so take care on loose sand, and keep to the cairned line rather than bushwhacking. The trail is also the preferred way down when combining Lamont with a longer day on the Pacific Crest Trail.
hazards: Steep, sandy trail that fades in places
Brush when you leave the trail
Optional class 3 scrambling on the summit blocks

review.notes: A search snippet suggested about 5 miles round trip and 2,100 ft, but that page returned 403 so it is not cited. Gain and distance are single-source, from user-logged climbs. Parking at about 5,500 ft comes from that same unopened snippet, so check it. Season skipped.

set.overview: Sawtooth Peak is the 8,000-foot summit just south of Lamont Peak in the Owens Peak Wilderness, reached from the Pacific Crest Trail. The standard way leaves the trail at a saddle and climbs a forested ridge on a steep, sandy social trail with a brushy final push. It finishes with a short class 2 scramble onto the summit block. Oak brush can be avoided with careful line choice, and the top gives wide views.
set.approach: Start at the Pacific Crest Trail crossing on Canebrake Road, part of the Chimney Peak back-country byway, and hike the trail south to the saddle immediately south of Sawtooth Peak. The crossing is unsigned and parking can be tricky. Leave the trail at the saddle and follow the social trail up the ridge to the summit block.
set.descent_text: Go back down the sandy social trail to the saddle and return north on the Pacific Crest Trail to Canebrake Road. The sandy slope is slippery on the way down, so keep your feet under you and avoid the brushy gullies beside the trail.
hazards: Steep sandy slope that slides underfoot
Oak and brush on the final push
Class 2 summit block with some exposure
Few trail signs at the Canebrake Road crossing

review.notes: Single-source gain and distance (peakery, 3 logged climbs). A search snippet of another page said about 5 mi and 2,500 ft but was not opened. Season skipped. The 'unsigned crossing' hazard is from a search snippet only; drop it if the reviewer wants opened-page evidence.

set.overview: Rockhouse Peak is a granite summit in the Domeland Wilderness on the Kern Plateau. Most of the trip follows trail through conifers and meadows, with an off-trail finish of a mile or more at class 2 to 3. From the saddle a class 3 route climbs the east side, while a class 2 gully on the north side offers an easier alternative. The south face holds real rock climbs, not a hiking route.
set.approach: From Kernville, drive Sherman Pass Road to Cherry Hill Road and then the Big Meadow road. Hike the Manter Creek Trail past Manter Meadow and Little Manter Meadow camp toward the creek confluence and the trail saddle, about 4.5 miles from Manter Meadow. Leave the trail there and follow the creek and a drainage cross-country to the base of the summit granite. Some stretches of trail are brushy and hard to follow.
set.descent_text: Retrace the route back over the saddle to the Manter Creek Trail and down to the trailhead. The north gully is a class 2 alternative for the descent from the summit. Take care on the slabs and ledges of the east face, which are exposed, and keep the route in mind for the brushy section near the creek.
hazards: Class 3 crack or ledges below the summit block
Unmaintained, faint trails and brush near the creek
Hot conditions in summer
Bears are present in the area

review.notes: Gain and distance skipped: figures range from 9 mi RT/2,200 ft from Manter Meadow to 16-18 mi RT/3,600-5,700 ft from Big Meadow, and the stored route does not name its trailhead. Season skipped (spring/fall is not a window).

set.approach: From Kernville take the road up Sherman Pass and Cherry Hill to the Big Meadow road, and park at the Big Meadow trailhead near 7,825 feet. Follow the Big Meadow Trail through forest, climbing gently to a saddle about 1.3 miles in, then leave it and follow the ridge northeast and east, keeping to the north side. The last section is a shallow chimney with large holds below the summit block.
set.descent_text: Retrace the off-trail ridge to the saddle and return along the Big Meadow Trail. Reverse the chimney moves carefully, since the exposed class 3 steps feel harder going down. Another option heads north-west to a saddle and picks up a trail toward Big Meadow.
hazards: Exposed class 3 to 4 moves in the summit chimney
Old trail signs are unclear and cow trails near Taylor Meadow confuse junctions
Steep south side with technical rock routes
Class 3 off-trail section; carry a map

evidence.fact: about 4.6 mi round trip from the upper trailhead; halved for one way = 2.3 mi

review.notes: Distance is single-source, round trip halved. Gain skipped: the only value is derived from elevations (about 980 ft), and trip reports with 17 mi / 4,300 ft combine Rockhouse. The northwest descent comes from a combined Rockhouse/Taylor report, not Taylor alone. Season skipped (a page only says summer).

set.overview: A straightforward trail hike to the 9,977-foot summit of Sirretta Peak on the Kern Plateau, starting from North Big Meadow. The route follows the Cannell Trail briefly, then the Sirretta Trail to Sirretta Pass, and finally a cairned use trail up the ridge to a summit made of a pile of boulders. Expect a little scrambling on the last stretch, with the easiest finish from the south or northeast side.
set.approach: From Kernville drive the Sherman Pass road, turn onto Cherry Hill Road, then onto the Big Meadow road and follow the signed turn to North Big Meadow, a dirt-road end with dispersed camping near 7,830 feet. Hike the Cannell Trail for about half a mile, cross a creek and a meadow, then turn right on the Sirretta Trail to Sirretta Pass. Cairns mark the start of the summit use trail.
set.descent_text: Return the way you came. Descending directly from the northeast side of the summit boulder pile is straightforward, then rejoin the Sirretta Trail at the pass and walk back down to the Cannell Trail and the trailhead.
hazards: Dirt bikes share the Sirretta Trail, especially on summer weekends
Mountain bikers use the Cannell Trail section
Afternoon thunderstorms are possible on the open summit ridge
West-side scramble to the top is harder class 2 than the northeast side

evidence.fact: about 2,200 ft gain, 7 mi round trip
7 mi round trip = 3.5 mi one way
7.5 mi round trip = 3.75 mi one way; midpoint 3.63 mi = 5.83 km

review.notes: Season skipped (a page says summer and fall, not a precise window). One report says Cherry Hill road, the other forest road numbering differs; I used the generic wording.
